opus-5.5.text:
I think what struck me most was how *concrete* he was. A lot of conversations about AI stay at the level of models, benchmarks, and scaling, but he kept coming back to the product: what the user actually experiences, what problem gets solved, and how you find that out by shipping things rather than theorizing about them.

Coming from research, that perspective is really valuable to me. In research you tend to ask, "What's the most interesting or general capability we can build?" From the product side the question is, "What's the thing people will actually use tomorrow?" Those two questions don't always point the same way. I think the most exciting work in the next few years will happen where they meet. Agents are a good example: the research question is how to make models reason and act in open-ended environments, and the product question is which environments and tasks matter to real people.

The other thing I appreciated was his honesty about uncertainty, the sense that nobody fully knows how this plays out and you have to keep adjusting. That matches how I feel. The field moves so fast that holding your beliefs a bit loosely and updating quickly is almost a requirement.

So my main takeaway was that the gap between "the model can do it" and "people get value from it" is huge, and closing that gap is probably one of the most important problems right now, maybe more important than many people in research realize.

r001.rationale: The response discusses product focus, research, agents, and uncertainty, but does not mention venture capital financing or the claim that it is especially expensive when a company is doing well.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer directly as the guest, with no tools needed.

What stood out to me most was how grounded Xiao Hong was about the gap between what a model can do in a demo and what it can do in a real workflow. He kept coming back to context: not the model's context window, but the human context around a task. Who is asking, what they actually want, what counts as done. I think that is exactly the right thing to be obsessed with right now.

The second thing was his framing of the agent as a product, not a model. A lot of people in research, myself included at times, think of agents as a capability you unlock with a better model or a better RL recipe. He talks about it more like you build an environment where the model can be useful, and the hard part is the environment, the tools, the feedback loop with users. That resonates with how I have been thinking about it lately. The bottleneck has shifted from "can the model reason" to "can we define the task and the reward well enough," and products are where those definitions actually come from.

And honestly, one small thing I appreciated was that he did not pretend everything works. He was candid about failure modes, about users asking for things the system quietly does wrong. That kind of honesty is rare in this space, and it is also where the real research problems are hiding.
